# Section A — As set

## Question 1 **[3]** &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">MAT 2023 · Q1H</span>

::: {.question}
Which of these triangles has the largest area? **(a)** $10,10,1$ &nbsp; **(b)** $10,10,5$ &nbsp;
**(c)** $10,10,10$ &nbsp; **(d)** $10,10,15$ &nbsp; **(e)** $10,10,19$. Give the letter, and say what the
largest possible area of a triangle with two sides of length $10$ is, and which triangle achieves it.
:::

Do **not** compute five areas. *The two sides of length $10$ are fixed, so use the enclosed-angle form of the
area, where everything except the angle is constant:*

$$\text{area}=\tfrac12\cdot10\cdot10\cdot\sin\theta=50\sin\theta . \tag*{[1]}$$

This is largest when $\sin\theta=1$, i.e. $\theta=90^\circ$, giving a maximum area of $\boxed{50}$, achieved
by the **right-angled isosceles** triangle — whose third side is $\sqrt{10^{2}+10^{2}}=10\sqrt2\approx14.14$.
**[1]**

So the winner is the option whose third side is closest to $10\sqrt2$, which is $15$: **(d)**. **[1]**

| third side | $1$ | $5$ | $10$ | $15$ | $19$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| area | $4.99$ | $24.21$ | $43.30$ | $\mathbf{49.61}$ | $29.66$ |

*Note that $19$ is nearly degenerate — the triangle is long and flat — which is why the largest third side
does not give the largest area. Area is not monotonic in the base.*

## Question 2 **[8]** &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock E · P2 Q20</span>

::: {.question}
**Statement $P$:** $ABC$ is a right-angled triangle. Which are true? **(1)** $P$ iff $ABC$ can be split by a
segment into two triangles each similar to $ABC$. **(2)** $P$ is necessary for $ABC$ to be splittable into
two triangles whose areas, with $ABC$'s, form a geometric sequence with ratio $\neq1$. **(3)** $P$ is
necessary for all four triangles made when a convex kite is cut by its diagonals. **(4)** $P$ is sufficient
for $ABC$ to be determined up to congruence by its hypotenuse and the median to it. **(5)** $P$ iff four
congruent copies of $ABC$ tile a rhombus edge-to-edge.
:::

$$\boxed{\textbf{F} \quad\text{— (1) and (3) only}} \tag*{[1]}$$

**(1) True.** **[2]**

*Forwards:* if $ABC$ is right-angled, the altitude from the right angle to the hypotenuse splits it into two
triangles each similar to $ABC$ — *each new triangle shares one acute angle with $ABC$ and has a right angle,
so all three angles match.*

*Backwards:* the segment must join a vertex to a point on the opposite side, making two **supplementary**
angles there. Both of those angles occur among the angles of $ABC$. *They cannot be two different angles of
$ABC$, because any two angles of a triangle sum to less than $180^\circ$.* So they are equal, hence each is
$90^\circ$, and $ABC$ is right-angled.

**(2) False.** **[2]** Let the area of $ABC$ be $S$ and let $r>1$ satisfy $r^{2}=r+1$, i.e.
$r=\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$. *A segment from a vertex to the opposite side can split a triangle in **any**
prescribed area ratio, because the two pieces share the same height and their areas are proportional to the
two parts of the base.* Split $ABC$ into pieces of area $\dfrac{S}{r^{2}}$ and $\dfrac{S}{r}$; these really do
add to $S$, since

$$\frac{1}{r^{2}}+\frac{1}{r}=\frac{1+r}{r^{2}}=\frac{r^{2}}{r^{2}}=1 .$$

Then $\dfrac{S}{r^{2}},\ \dfrac{S}{r},\ S$ is geometric with ratio $r\neq1$. *This works for **any** triangle,
so being right-angled is not necessary.*

**(3) True.** **[1]** The diagonals of a convex kite are **perpendicular**, so each of the four triangles has
a right angle where the diagonals cross.

**(4) False.** **[1]** *In any right-angled triangle the midpoint of the hypotenuse is equidistant from all
three vertices, so the median to the hypotenuse is always exactly half of it.* Knowing the hypotenuse
therefore already tells you the median — it adds nothing — and the hypotenuse alone certainly does not fix the
triangle. (See Question 5.)

**(5) False.** **[1]** A counterexample is built in Question 6: four congruent copies of a triangle with sides
$1,2,\sqrt7$ tile a rhombus of side $2$, and that triangle is not right-angled.

*The shape of this question is worth noting: two of the five are settled by a construction you can draw, two
by a standard fact, and only (1) needs an argument in both directions.*

# Section B — The midpoint quadrilateral

## Question 3 **[10]**

::: {.question}
$ABCD$ convex, $E,F,G,H$ the midpoints of $AB,BC,CD,DA$. **(a)** Show $EFGH$ is always a parallelogram with
sides parallel to the diagonals and half their length. **(b)** $EFGH$ is a rhombus iff the diagonals of
$ABCD$ are equal. **(c)** $EFGH$ is a rectangle iff the diagonals are perpendicular. **(d)** The condition
for a square, and an $ABCD$ which is not a square but whose $EFGH$ is.
:::

**(a)** *By the midpoint theorem applied to triangle $ABC$, the segment joining the midpoints of two sides is
parallel to the third side and half its length:*

$$\overrightarrow{EF}=\tfrac12\overrightarrow{AC},\qquad
\overrightarrow{FG}=\tfrac12\overrightarrow{BD},\qquad
\overrightarrow{GH}=-\tfrac12\overrightarrow{AC},\qquad
\overrightarrow{HE}=-\tfrac12\overrightarrow{BD}. \tag*{[2]}$$

Since $\overrightarrow{EF}=-\overrightarrow{GH}$, opposite sides are equal and parallel, so $EFGH$ is a
parallelogram — **for every $ABCD$, with no condition at all**. **[1]**

**(b)** A parallelogram is a rhombus exactly when two **adjacent** sides are equal. Here
$EF=\tfrac12AC$ and $FG=\tfrac12BD$, so **[2]**

$$EF=FG\iff \tfrac12AC=\tfrac12BD\iff AC=BD .$$

*Both directions come for free from that single chain of equivalences — which is why writing the lengths in
terms of the diagonals is the whole of the work.* **[1]**

**(c)** A parallelogram is a rectangle exactly when two adjacent sides are **perpendicular**. Since $EF$ is
parallel to $AC$ and $FG$ is parallel to $BD$, **[2]**

$$EF\perp FG\iff AC\perp BD .$$

**(d)** A square is a rhombus **and** a rectangle, so the condition is that the diagonals of $ABCD$ are
**equal in length and perpendicular**. **[1]**

An example that is **not** a square is the kite

$$A=(0,0),\qquad B=(1,2),\qquad C=(4,0),\qquad D=(1,-2).$$

*Its diagonals are $AC$ along the $x$-axis and $BD$ along the line $x=1$: both have length $4$ and they are
perpendicular, but they do not bisect each other, so the kite is not a square* — indeed
$AB=DA=\sqrt5$ while $BC=CD=\sqrt{13}$.

Its midpoint quadrilateral has all four sides $2$ and both diagonals $2\sqrt2$, so $EFGH$ **is** a square.
**[1]**

*The point: the conditions in (b), (c) and (d) are conditions on the **diagonals** of $ABCD$, and the
diagonals say nothing about whether $ABCD$ itself is a nice shape.*

# Section C — Deductions and constructions

## Question 4 **[4]**

::: {.question}
$\angle A=30^\circ$, $AB=x^{2}$, $BC=2x$, $x>0$, with exactly two non-congruent triangles. **(a)** Find the
exact set of $x$. **(b)** Which of **A** $1<x<5$, **B** $2<x<3$, **C** $3<x<5$, **D** $0<x<3$, **E** $x>3$
can be deduced, and why not the others?
:::

**(a)** *This is SSA: the given angle is not between the two given sides, so the number of triangles is
decided by comparing $BC$ with the distance from $B$ to the ray $AC$.* That distance is

$$h=AB\sin A=x^{2}\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac{x^{2}}{2}. \tag*{[1]}$$

Two non-congruent triangles exist exactly when $h<BC<AB$: **[1]**

$$\frac{x^{2}}{2}<2x<x^{2}.$$

Since $x>0$ we may divide by $x$ throughout: the left gives $x<4$, the right gives $x>2$, so **[1]**

$$\boxed{2<x<4}.$$

**(b)** **A.** *"Can be deduced" asks for a **necessary** condition — a statement implied by $2<x<4$ — which
means the option whose interval **contains** $(2,4)$.* Only $1<x<5$ does. **[1]**

| | interval | contains $(2,4)$? |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | $(1,5)$ | **yes** |
| **B** | $(2,3)$ | no — fails at $x=3.5$ |
| **C** | $(3,5)$ | no — fails at $x=2.5$ |
| **D** | $(0,3)$ | no — fails at $x=3.5$ |
| **E** | $(3,\infty)$ | no — fails at $x=2.5$ |

*B, C, D and E all overlap $(2,4)$, which is exactly the trap: overlapping is not containing. A value of $x$
in $(2,4)$ but outside the option would make the "deduction" false.*

## Question 5 **[4]**

::: {.question}
Prove that in any right-angled triangle the median to the hypotenuse is half the hypotenuse. Hence explain
why the hypotenuse and that median together do not determine the triangle up to congruence, and give two
non-congruent right-angled triangles with hypotenuse $10$.
:::

**The proof.** Let the right angle be at $C$ and let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$. *Thales' theorem says the
circle with diameter $AB$ passes through every point from which $AB$ subtends a right angle — so $C$ lies on
the circle with diameter $AB$, whose centre is $M$.* Hence **[2]**

$$MA=MB=MC=\tfrac12 AB .$$

*(Equivalently: draw through $M$ the lines parallel to the two legs; they cut the triangle into four congruent
pieces and show $MC=MA=MB$ directly.)*

**Why the data is not enough.** The median is **always** $\tfrac12AB$, so once the hypotenuse is given, the
median is forced and carries **no extra information**. *The two measurements are really one measurement, and
one length cannot determine a triangle.* **[1]**

Two non-congruent examples with hypotenuse $10$, and median $5$ in both: **[1]**

$$\text{legs }6,\,8 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \text{legs }5\sqrt2,\,5\sqrt2 .$$

*Both are right-angled with hypotenuse $10$, since $6^{2}+8^{2}=100$ and
$\left(5\sqrt2\right)^{2}+\left(5\sqrt2\right)^{2}=100$. Their areas are $24$ and $25$, so they are not
congruent.*

---

## Question 6 **[5]**

::: {.question}
A rhombus has side $2$ and acute angle $60^\circ$. **(a)** Join the midpoints of one pair of opposite sides,
then cut each piece along its longer diagonal; show this gives four congruent triangles filling the rhombus,
and find their side lengths. **(b)** Show the triangle is not right-angled, and say which statement of
Question 2 this disproves.
:::

**(a)** Joining the midpoints of one pair of opposite sides cuts the rhombus into **two congruent
parallelograms**, each with adjacent sides $1$ and $2$ — *the cut is parallel to the other pair of sides and
halves them, so each piece has the rhombus's $60^\circ$ and $120^\circ$ angles.* **[1]**

Cutting a parallelogram along a diagonal always gives two congruent triangles, so all four are congruent and
together they fill the rhombus exactly. **[1]**

Taking the **longer** diagonal — the one opposite the $120^\circ$ angle — the triangle has sides $1$ and $2$
enclosing $120^\circ$, and third side $d$ with **[1]**

$$d^{2}=1^{2}+2^{2}-2(1)(2)\cos120^\circ=1+4+2=7,$$

so the side lengths are $\boxed{1,\ 2,\ \sqrt7}$.

**(b)** $1^{2}+2^{2}=5\neq7=\left(\sqrt7\right)^{2}$, so the converse of Pythagoras fails and the triangle is
**not right-angled**. **[1]**

Four congruent copies of a non-right-angled triangle therefore tile a rhombus, which disproves the
"**only if**" half of **statement (5)** in Question 2. **[1]**

*Note which half: the construction says nothing about whether right-angled triangles can tile a rhombus —
it only shows that tiling one does not force a right angle.*

---

::: {.callout-tip}
## What this sheet was testing

1. **Area is $\tfrac12ab\sin\theta$** — with two sides fixed it is the **angle** that is free, and it peaks
   at $90^\circ$, not at the largest third side (Q1).
2. **Named figures settle false statements.** A kite, a non-square rectangle, a $1,2,\sqrt7$ triangle — each
   kills a statement in one line (Q2, Q6).
3. **The midpoint quadrilateral turns diagonal facts into side facts**: equal diagonals give a rhombus,
   perpendicular diagonals a rectangle, both a square (Q3).
4. **"Can be deduced" means necessary, so the answer is the larger set** — overlapping is not containing
   (Q4).
5. **Watch for data that is secretly one number**: the median to the hypotenuse is determined by the
   hypotenuse, so it adds nothing (Q5, and statement (4) of Q2).
:::

:::
